title: Lesson 77 - Where Do We Want to Be in a Year?

lines.speaker: Owen
lines.text: A year from now, I don’t want us simply to say that we stayed busier. I want to know whether limited evening bookings can support the café without weakening the daytime service people already rely on.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: Then the destination is not “open more evenings.” It is “reach an evidence-based decision about a limited evening option while protecting the core business.”

lines.speaker: Owen
lines.text: Exactly. What I need you to understand is that stability counts as success too. If the evidence says evenings create too much strain, choosing not to expand would still be a useful result.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: Good. Otherwise every milestone will quietly assume growth is the answer. What would we need to have learned by this time next year?

lines.speaker: Owen
lines.text: We’ll have compared genuine demand, direct costs, staff capacity and the effect on the following morning. We’ll also have recorded why groups chose us or decided not to book.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: And at that point, we’ll be using one of three clear models: no evening bookings, occasional bookings under strict conditions or a small recurring schedule.

lines.speaker: Owen
lines.text: I like that. We are not promising the third model. We are promising that the choice will be based on more than a few enthusiastic messages.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: A year from now, we want to be able to explain the decision to staff in one page: what we tested, what happened, what we learned and what we will do next.

lines.speaker: Owen
lines.text: Can we agree that staff recovery is a success measure, not a problem to discuss after the financial numbers?

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: Yes. If people are regularly arriving tired for the morning shift, the plan is off track even if every evening slot is booked.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: Let’s work backward. By the end of the first month, we’ll have classified the inquiries we already receive instead of asking customers to complete a new survey.

lines.speaker: Owen
lines.text: That keeps the first step light. We’ll be recording group size, preferred day, requested service and whether the inquiry became a booking somewhere else.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: By month three, we’ll have drafted a small pilot with a budget ceiling, staffing rule, limited menu and clear stop conditions. Drafted does not mean approved.

lines.speaker: Owen
lines.text: Right. During the next stage, we’ll be checking the proposal with the people who would actually work the shifts, not just with customers who like the idea.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: If a pilot is approved, by month six we’ll have completed enough trial evenings to compare setup time, service time, cleanup and next-morning impact.

lines.speaker: Owen
lines.text: If it isn’t approved, we’ll have documented why and what evidence would justify reopening the question. A “no for now” should not disappear into memory.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: Our final milestone is a decision review. We’ll know we’re on track when each stage produces a record that the next stage can actually use.

lines.speaker: Owen
lines.text: From now on, let’s label every item as a goal, milestone, assumption or decision. That should stop a possible idea from appearing on the schedule as a commitment.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: I’ll turn this into a one-page roadmap. Let me finish the first draft before we debate individual menu items; otherwise we’ll solve details before agreeing on the destination.

lines.speaker: Owen
lines.text: Agreed. The first milestone is not an evening event. It is a reliable picture of demand and capacity, ready for a proposal discussion in four weeks.
